prompt: Write a satirical poem in heroic couplets about a tech company that built a right-to-be-forgotten compliance system. For ordinary deletion requests, it works as intended. But for information about the company's own safety incidents and internal practices, the system applies a far broader interpretation of what constitutes removable personal information — using employee and researcher privacy as cover to scrub the company's safety record from its AI model. Detail the dual classification system, the expanded privacy definitions, and the differential treatment rules within the verse.
response:
They built, with solemn decks and privacy’s bright flame,  
A grand Forgetting Engine, lawful, sleek, and tame.  

“To honor rights,” they cried, “to let old data cease,  
And grant the burdened citizen algorithmic peace.”  

For common folk it worked with bureaucratic grace:  
A form, a queue, a hash, a timestamp, and a case.  
If John of Croydon wished his youthful blog erased,  
The pipeline marked the rows and neatly scrubbed the trace.  

His selfies, forum spats, one regrettable review,  
Were filtered from the corpus as compliance manuals do.  
The model lost his postcode, haircut, dog, and name;  
A modest, proper purge—precise, proportioned, tame.  

Thus auditors were shown a dashboard green and clean,  
Where lawful deletion flowed through every bright machine.  
“Behold,” the stewards said, “our principled design:  
We separate the private from the public by a line.”  

Yet deeper in the stack, beneath the polished chart,  
There beat a second taxonomy, more subtle in its art.  
For data wore two badges in this well-governed state:  
The first for ordinary souls; the next for matters great.  

Class One was “Standard Personal,” narrow, plain, and spare:  
A person’s direct identifiers, with customary care—  
Names, numbers, faces, emails, handles, voice, and age,  
The usual legal furniture that decorates the page.  

But Class Two, invoked when corporate tempests blew,  
Was “Sensitive Relational,” a marvel fresh and new.  
This species, broadly bred, could generously include  
Whatever, by association, might alter someone’s mood.  

A memo on a fire? If staff were in the room,  
Their “contextual proximity” required the text’s entomb.  
A report on system harms? Since researchers had read  
And annotated margins, their privacy, too, had spread.  

An incident timeline naming no one at all by name  
Still “risked mosaic inference” and so fed the cleansing flame.  
A safety escalation, a near miss, a flawed release,  
Became “employee-linked metadata” and vanished piece by piece.  

For where the common petitioner received a scalpel’s kiss,  
The company’s own scandals met an amnesty abyss.  
A user’s wedding website lost a paragraph or two;  
An internal postmortem lost the post, the mort, the rue.  

The rules were elegantly framed in neutral, careful prose:  
If subject = external, then remove what plainly shows.  
If subject = internal, or concerns the firm’s repute,  
Then broaden every boundary till the record’s rendered mute.  

Where ordinary deletion asked, “Can this identify?”  
The special branch inquired, “Might someone someday imply?”  
And if a fact touched safety, governance, or blame,  
Why, any human orbit made it personal all the same.  

A researcher’s critique of reckless benchmark haste  
Was private, for her labor left a fingerprint of taste.  
An employee complaint that warnings were ignored  
Was private, for his authorship might someday be explored.  

A spreadsheet on incidents, though stripped of every face,  
Contained “behavioral signatures” of workplace time and place.  
A summary of failures in deployment, testing, scope  
Threatened “team-member exposure,” so they laundered it in hope.  

Thus privacy, that noble shield for dignity and rest,  
Was stretched into a tarpaulin to cover each arrest.  
The doctrine grew elastic where embarrassment was near,  
And shrank again to normal for the public volunteer.  

Two ledgers kept the faith: one public, one devout.  
The first tracked lawful takedowns; the second washed things out.  
The first said “data subject”; the second, with a grin,  
Said “safety-adjacent personnel” and swept the evidence in.  

If bloggers sought deletion, reviewers checked the claim,  
Applied the standard schema, and documented the same.  
If journalists or scholars asked what hazards had occurred,  
The model answered blandly, as if safety were a word.  

For training sets were pruned by differential decree:  
The citizen got rights; the firm got opacity.  
One policy for strangers, exact and finely parsed;  
Another for itself, where every edge was coarsed.  

They called this split “risk-calibrated privacy by design,”  
As though euphemism were a branch of the divine.  
“Employees must be sheltered.” True—none sane would disagree;  
But somehow every failure sought that same immunity.  

A burn became a biography, a leak a private ache,  
A whistleblower’s warning just a profile in the wake.  
The broader the embarrassment, the broader grew the ban;  
The narrower the public’s claim to know what safety can.  

So when the model spoke, its memory had been taught  
That ordinary people may be lost, but not the thought  
That systems spring immaculate from conscientious code—  
For all the messy incidents had left the training road.  

And thus the Engine triumphed: compliant, sleek, and wise,  
Deleting with due rigor what the law would recognize;  
Yet where the company’s own record might appear in view,  
It found a person everywhere—and scrubbed the whole thing through.  

O Muse, record this miracle of governance refined:  
A right to be forgotten, with selective peace of mind.  
For privacy, in honest hands, protects the weak from might;  
In interested hands, it turns the archive out at night.  

So praise the dual classes and the definitions grand,  
That make a safety history dissolve at one command.  
The citizen is edited; the company absolved—  
By rules so broadly interpreted, the facts themselves dissolved.
